n: In this lecture we will study poisonous compounds containing barium and lead and the methods of their analysis, including tetraethyl lead. Key words and expressions: mineralisate, barium, lead and the fractional method. The aim: to become familiar with the reagents for masking interfering ions in the fractional method. We will also study the toxicological significance and analysis of barium and lead in the precipitate.

First let us consider the significance of metallic poisons. Metal-containing substances occur in the body as part of trace elements and enzymes. Therefore determining the amount of a poisonous cation is one of the essential requirements. Salts of heavy metals are widely used in agriculture as micro-fertilisers and pesticides, reagents and catalysts, and in industry as raw materials. Poisoning with compounds of arsenic, mercury, manganese, lead and zinc occurs frequently.

Lethal doses of metallic poisons. For chromium and manganese, the higher-valency compounds have the stronger action. For mercury LD50 = 0.2-0.3 g, for ZnCl2 5.0, for KMnO4 15-20 g. For arsenic and antimony this figure is 0.08-0.1 g, for thallium 0.5 g, for chromium 0.2-1 g, for cadmium 0.03 g. Organic compounds of mercury have a strong toxic action.

t: Colour of Vomit and Signs of Poisoning
n: General signs of poisoning: thirst, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain and internal bleeding. The vomit corresponds to the metal compound. With chromium and copper the vomit is green, with manganese brown. With lead, black spots appear on the gums, and with bismuth and mercury, white ones. The victim feels a metallic taste in the mouth.

Metal poisoning has other features as well. Cadmium causes bleeding from the internal organs, and in copper poisoning there is nosebleed. Copper and zinc compounds raise body temperature to 40 °C and above. Arsenic, lead and mercury have the property of accumulating in the body. Metals cause fat to accumulate in the parenchymatous organs. Poisoning with arsenic and mercury ends in death in 50 percent of cases.

t: Objects of Examination and Colour of the Precipitate
n: Objects of examination and colour of the precipitate. As objects of forensic chemical examination, the stomach, small and large intestine, liver and gallbladder, and kidney are taken. Urine, spleen, vomit, hair, nails and bones are also examined. The precipitate isolated from the mineralisate is white, depending on its composition, and may contain sulphates of barium, lead and calcium. If cations of chromium, copper, iron and aluminium precipitate together, the precipitate becomes dirty bluish.

There are two methods of determining metals. The hydrogen sulphide method is based on separating cations in the mineralisate by analytical groups with the help of group precipitants and solvents. It was used in forensic chemical practice until the 1970s, has many disadvantages and is not used now. Now in forensic chemical laboratories the particular fractional method is widely used to determine cations.

The principle of the fractional method is as follows. It is based on isolating cations from the mineralisate by extraction and re-extraction and identifying them with specific and sensitive reactions. In most cases, complex compounds are formed to eliminate the influence of interfering cations. Oxidation-reduction reactions, change of pH, obtaining a small volume of mineralisate, and dilution are also used. This method was proposed by Doctor of Chemical Sciences A.N. Krylova.

Masking has a two-stage working procedure. In the fractional method, the analysis of metals proceeds in two stages. First the interfering ions are removed with a reagent, then a reagent giving a colour or a precipitate is added. That is, masking is the elimination of the influence of ions that interfere with identification. In the scheme, the interfering ion is masked, a sensitive reagent is added, and a colour or precipitate is observed.

t: Bases of Masking and an Example
n: The bases of masking: formation of a stable complex, change of valency and change of the pH of the medium. Example: in identifying Co2+ with thiocyanate, Fe3+ interferes. This is because (NH4)2Co(CNS)4 gives a blue colour, whereas Fe(CNS)3 gives a blood-red colour. Fluoride and phosphates mask Fe3+, the complex [FeF6]3- formed being colourless.

Demasking is the release of a masked ion from the masking reagent. Citric acid is used for masking Bi, Cu, Fe, Sb, Hg, Ag, Cd. Tartaric acid is used for masking Cu, Fe, Al, Bi, Cd, Hg, Pb, Zn. In masking, complexone III, that is, Trilon B, and citric, tartaric and ascorbic acids are widely used.

The general list of masking reagents. To mask interfering ions, cyanides, fluorides, phosphates, thiosulphates, thiourea and other reagents are used. Cyanides form various complexes with the interfering ions Cu2+, Co2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Ni2+, Zn2+, Cd2+, Hg2+, Ag+. The list also includes hydroxylamine, glycerol, ascorbic acid, complexones, and citric and oxalic acids.

Masking with cyanides proceeds in two stages: first copper(II) is reduced, then the complex ion forms. The sequence of reactions: CuSO4 + 2KCN → Cu(CN)2 + K2SO4, then 2Cu(CN)2 → 2CuCN + (CN)2, then CuCN + 3KCN → K3[Cu(CN)4]. Remember: cyanide must not be added to an acidic solution, because volatile, poisonous hydrogen cyanide forms. For this reason, experiments with cyanides are always carried out in a fume cupboard.

Fluorides, phosphates and thiosulphates. Fluorides form the colourless stable complex [FeF6]3- with Fe3+ ions. Phosphates and phosphoric acid in an acidic medium form a colourless complex with Fe3+, given in the table as [Fe(PO4)2]3-. Thiosulphates mask silver, lead, copper and iron ions. They give the complexes [Ag(S2O3)3]4-, [Pb(S2O3)3]4- and [Fe(S2O3)2]-. Copper is first reduced to Cu+.

Hydroxylamine, thiourea and glycerol. Hydroxylamine reduces Fe3+, oxidises the ions AsO2- and SbO2-, and with cobalt gives the complex [Co(NH2OH)6]2+. Excess hydroxylamine is eliminated with formaldehyde, forming formaldoxime. Thiourea masks the ions of bismuth, iron, antimony, cadmium, mercury and silver. Glycerol masks the ions of bismuth, lead and cadmium.

Complexones, citric and oxalic acids. Complexone III, that is, Trilon B, forms stable inner complexes with metal ions and, regardless of valency, reacts in a 1:1 ratio. Citric acid masks the ions of bismuth, copper, iron(III), antimony(III), cadmium, mercury and silver. Oxalates give water-soluble stable complexes with the ions of copper, iron, aluminium, bismuth, cadmium, mercury, lead and zinc. Ascorbic acid, on the basis of its reducing properties, masks Fe3+ and Sn4+ ions.

Now barium compounds and their uses. Barium carbonate mixed with flour is used to destroy mice and rats. Children who eat it may cause an accident. Barium chloride, nitrate and hydroxide are used as reagents. BaCO3 is used in the production of glass and porcelain, and BaCl2 in the textile and rubber industries. BaCO3 and barium selenite, that is, BaSeO3, are used in agriculture against pests. Barium salts are also used in the production of paper and securities.

Toxicological significance of barium. Barium compounds are poisonous: for example, 0.8-0.9 g of BaCO3 is toxic. In poisoning with barium salts, the heart muscle fails and death occurs with consciousness retained. Signs: burning in the stomach and mouth, salivation, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea. The rhythm of the heartbeat changes and blood pressure rises. Dizziness, ringing in the ears and impaired vision are observed, and death occurs from cardiac paralysis.

t: Separating the BaSO4 and PbSO4 Precipitate
n: Separating the BaSO4 and PbSO4 precipitate. After denitration of the mineralisate, the precipitate may contain lead sulphate together with barium sulphate. The precipitate is washed with hot acidified ammonium acetate. In this process BaSO4 remains on the filter, and PbSO4 passes into the filtrate. The solution is tested for the lead cation, and the precipitate for barium.

t: Identity Reactions of Barium: Flame and BaS
n: Identity reactions of barium: flame and BaS. When heated on a platinum wire in a gas flame, the flame is coloured green, BaSO4 being partly reduced to BaS. BaCl2 is obtained from BaS with HCl. From it, BaSO4 is formed with Na2SO4, or Ba(IO3)2 with KIO3. Ba(IO3)2 is observed under the microscope as colourless prismatic crystals spread out in spheroids.

The recrystallisation reaction of BaSO4. The precipitate under test is placed on a microscope slide, and 2-3 drops of concentrated H2SO4 are added. Then it is heated until white vapours of SO3 appear. The plate is cooled for 15-20 minutes and examined under the microscope. As a result, colourless small crystals of BaSO4 in the shape of a lens or a "+" sign are seen.

t: Reactions Characteristic of the Ba2+ Ion
n: Reactions characteristic of the Ba2+ ion. With chromates, a yellow precipitate of BaCrO4 forms, insoluble in acetic acid. With sodium rhodizonate, a reddish-brown precipitate forms, and with 1 drop of HCl it turns bright red. If the colour was produced by strontium, it disappears under the action of hydrochloric acid.

Let us consider the reaction of Ba2+ with sodium rhodizonate separately. The barium ion gives a reddish-brown precipitate with sodium rhodizonate. Under the action of 1 drop of hydrochloric acid, the colour of the precipitate turns bright red. If the colour was produced by strontium, it disappears under the action of hydrochloric acid. In this way barium is distinguished from strontium.

Quantitative determination of barium is carried out by two methods: gravimetric and volumetric. In the gravimetric method, the precipitate is dissolved in an ammoniacal solution of Trilon B and filtered, in order to purify it from SiO2, and Fe3+ and Ca2+ salts. The filtrate is acidified, the BaSO4 is isolated, dried and weighed. In the volumetric method, the precipitate is dissolved in Trilon B of exact concentration, and the excess Trilon B is titrated with ZnCl2 using eriochrome blue indicator. The blue colour should change to red.

Now lead compounds. Among them, the salts arsenate, acetate, chromate, chloride, carbonate and nitrate have great toxicological significance. Metallic lead is widely used in printing and in making accumulators. 2PbCO3·Pb(OH)2, that is, white lead, and PbSO4, that is, red lead, are used in preparing paints. TEL is added to petrol as an anti-knock agent. Basic lead acetate is used in medicine. Poisoning occurs in daily life, industry and agriculture.

t: Action of Lead in the Body
n: The action of lead in the body. The lead ion, combining with the sulphydryl and other functional groups of enzymes and proteins, disrupts the work of the central nervous system. After absorption into the blood, 90 percent of lead binds to erythrocytes. The main part of lead compounds is excreted in faeces.

Determining lead with dithizone. A chloroform solution of dithizone colours the chloroform layer red. To mask interfering ions, KCN or hydroxylamine is added. The chloroform layer is shaken with nitric acid, which is called re-extraction. The aqueous layer is tested additionally.

Let us consider once again the reaction of Pb2+ with dithizone. A chloroform solution of dithizone with the lead cation colours the chloroform layer red. The reaction proceeds at pH = 7-10. To mask interfering ions, KCN or hydroxylamine is added. The reaction has negative forensic chemical significance. When the chloroform layer is shaken with nitric acid, the lead passes into the aqueous layer.

Microcrystalline reactions of lead. In the first, 1-2 drops of 1 percent copper acetate are dried, 2-3 drops of 30 percent acetic acid and a crystal of KNO2 are added. As a result, black-brown cubic crystals of K2Cu[Pb(NO2)6] form. In the second, 4-5 drops of aqueous solution are dried, and 2-3 drops of 30 percent acetic acid, CsCl and KI are added.

Precipitation reactions of lead. With hydrogen sulphide water, 3-5 drops, a black precipitate of PbS forms. With 5 percent potassium chromate, 3-5 drops, a yellow-orange precipitate of PbCrO4 forms. With 10 percent sulphuric acid, 5 drops, a white precipitate of PbSO4 forms.

The dichromate-iodometric determination of lead consists of three stages. The method is based on obtaining a precipitate of PbCrO4. Then the dichromate, in the presence of KI and H2SO4, liberates iodine. The liberated iodine is titrated with sodium thiosulphate.

Quantitative determination of lead. The first method is measuring the coloured solution obtained with dithizone by the photoelectrocolorimetric method, that is, PEC. The second method is complexometric, that is, volumetric-trilonometric, the indicator being eriochrome black. The third is the dichromate-iodometric method: a precipitate of PbCrO4 is obtained, iodine is liberated and titrated with sodium thiosulphate.

Tetraethyl lead, that is, TEL. It is an organometallic compound added to fuel as an anti-knock agent, which protects internal combustion engines from failure. A colourless liquid with a nauseating smell, insoluble in water, it dissolves well in organic solvents, especially in petrol. The boiling point is 198-200 °C with decomposition. On burning it forms a long, thin flame and yellowish-white smoke. Since the smoke consists of PbO particles, it has a toxic effect.

t: Leaded Fuel and Materials for Examination
n: Leaded fuel and materials for examination. Petrols and kerosenes containing TEL are called leaded petrol. To distinguish such fuels, various dyes are added. They lead to different kinds of poisoning. As materials, leaded fuels, clothing and the internal organs of the deceased are sent to forensic laboratories.

t: Amount of TEL and Isolation Indicators
n: The key figures for TEL. If 100 g of object contains 0.3 g of TEL, signs of poisoning are considered to be present. Usually 100 ml of distillate is collected and kept closed for 30 minutes. For a petrol sample, petrol, 20 ml, is mixed with a 4 percent alcoholic solution of iodine, 20 ml, and evaporated after 30 minutes.

Isolating TEL from the object. From the internal organs of a corpse, meat and foodstuffs, TEL is isolated by steam distillation. The distillate is collected in a saturated alcoholic solution of iodine. Usually 100 ml of distillate is collected, kept closed for 30 minutes and evaporated to dryness on a water bath. Under the action of iodine, TEL is converted into lead iodide, that is, PbI2. The PbI2 in the residue is dissolved in nitric acid and dried. Pb(NO3)2 is dissolved in water and tested with the reactions for Pb2+.

t: Determining TEL in Plant Objects and in Petrol
n: Determining TEL in plant objects and in petrol. From flour, bread and groats, the object is soaked in chloroform or another organic solvent for 2 hours. 1 g of iodine is added to the filtrate, and after 30 minutes it is evaporated. The residue is broken down with sulphuric and nitric acids, that is, mineralised, purified from nitrogen oxides and tested for Pb2+. For petrol and kerosene, petrol, 20 ml, is mixed with 4 percent iodine alcohol, 20 ml, evaporated after 30 minutes, and the residue is tested for Pb2+. If 100 g of object contains 0.3 g of TEL, signs of poisoning are considered to be present.

In conclusion. In the precipitate, BaSO4 and PbSO4 are separated with hot ammonium acetate, that is, acidified with acetic acid. Barium is identified by the flame and by crystals of Ba(IO3)2 and BaSO4, and lead by dithizone and microcrystals. In the fractional method the interfering ions are masked first, then the sensitive reagent is added. TEL is isolated by steam distillation or with the help of an organic solvent, converted by iodine into PbI2, then tested for Pb2+. For self-review, go over the masking reagents, the separation of BaSO4 and PbSO4, and the quantitative methods for Ba and Pb.
